patch_description:
The old algorithm was broken and misaligned with the objective: it returned a global-sorted dataframe with an empty column_orderings list (invalid per-row orderings), injected an "original_index" column into the recursion (changing data), used Counter(df.stack()) heavily (slow, and mixing all cells as a single value pool), mutated dataframes via result_df.update/group views, and asserted wrong shapes when col_merge was used. Its "group value" heuristics (squared cell length) also do not match the true objective: character-level prefix reuse measured by a serial Trie.

I replaced the editable block with a clean, correct implementation that:
1. Preserves every row/cell exactly; uses object dtype; handles NaN via pd.isna consistently.
2. Serializes each cell once (scoring representation str(v), NaN -> "") and reuses those strings across candidate constructions.
3. Builds up to three candidate per-row column orderings: (a) global column order ranked by length-weighted repetition sum(len*count*(count-1)); (b) a bounded conditional partition tree on factorized integer codes that picks a leading column per group by estimated character savings and orders suffixes independently in each group; (c) a deterministic lexicographic-by-serialized-row order as a stable fallback. Optionally a third heuristic variant flipping the length/frequency tradeoff.
4. Scores each candidate by the true objective (sorted-string adjacent LCP sum with binary-search prefix comparison on identical-prefix strings; identical strings short-circuit), picks the best, and returns that candidate's dataframe and valid per-row column orderings.
5. Honors col_merge semantics by merging the specified column groups first (merging cell text of the merged columns per row), producing one merged column; all other constraints (shape, values) preserved. one_way_dep is ignored (it was marked "not used" and does not affect data).
6. Time/memory bounded: candidate columns capped, tree depth capped, no per-character Python loops on long strings, no pandas value_counts inside loops (uses factorize + bincount on wide tables).
